item.title: Scottish roundup: Flying Falkirk hit five to shatter Hearts’ long unbeaten home run
item.description: Falkirk leapfrog their hosts with 5-2 rout at Tynecastle Liam Scales gives Celtic 1-0 home win over Kilmarnock Rampant Falkirk obliterated Hearts ’ 18-month unbeaten home record in the Scottish Premiership with a stunning 5-2 win at Tynecastle on Sunday as they leapfrogged their hosts into third place. Wouter Vrancken’s beleaguered side, missing 11 players through injury, were in disarray as swashbuckling Falkirk romped into a five-goal lead early in the second half through Finley Barbrook, Owen Eames, Liam Henderson and Jacob Murrell’s double. Hearts hit back through the substitute Sabri Guendouz and a Cláudio Braga penalty, but Falkirk were well worthy of making it five top-flight wins in a row for the first time since 1995. item.title: 2,800-year-old Siberian tomb reveals cannabis seeds and traces in human hair
item.description: A groundbreaking archaeological find at Tunnug 1 in southern Siberia unveiled cannabis seeds within a prince's tomb, dating back 2,800 years. This tomb is tied to intricate funerary rites, including horse sacrifices. Notably, preserved human hair revealed traces of cannabis, hinting at its psychoactive use, which underscores cannabis's significant role in ancient burial customs. Researchers plan to conduct further DNA analysis to deepen the understanding of its historical relevance.

item.title: The Guardian view on a tale of two activists: Joshua Wong and Au Kam San should not be behind bars | Editorial
item.description: The latest vindictive prosecutions and harsh sentences in Hong Kong and Macau are further testimony to China’s ruthless suppression of dissent One is internationally famous – he was once dubbed “the Face of Protest” by Time magazine – and the other is little known outside his home town. What Joshua Wong and Au Kam San share, beyond the harsh sentences they received last week, is that they represent the spirit of dissent that Beijing is determined to crush. Mr Wong , who has been in prison for six years, should have walked free next January – not free to fight for Hong Kong’s rights, which China has suppressed so decisively, but at least to walk the streets of the city he loves. Instead, a court last Thursday sentenced the 30-year-old, an activist from the age of 14 , to another 10 years . He is the only person to have been prosecuted twice under the draconian national security law (NSL). item.title: The Guardian view on Ordnance Survey maps: still a superior way to navigate the landscape | Editorial
item.description: The 225th anniversary of the organisation’s first publication is an opportunity to celebrate its unique contribution to our sense of place In his one-paragraph short story , On Exactitude in Science, Jorge Luis Borges imagines an empire in which the level of cartographical ambition is so high that a map is made on a one-to-one scale with the imperial territory. The quest for perfect accuracy doesn’t end well. But the earliest map-makers for Ordnance Survey, which this week marked the 225th anniversary of its first publication, might have empathised with the obsessive dedication. The 1801 OS map of Kent was 10 years in the making, its military-led production inspired by fears of Napoleonic invasion. But as Rachel Hewitt points out in Map of a Nation , her stirring account of the Ordnance Survey’s early years, its genesis also lay in an Enlightenment-based enthusiasm for comprehending and accurately representing reality. item.title: What are you yearning for? We took to the streets to find out
item.description: Longing for someone – or something – can be even more thrilling than getting what you want. That knowledge has inspired endless movies, but what do real people yearn for? We asked the question in Glasgow In a world of instant gratification, is it any surprise that many of us have fallen back in love with the idea of “yearning”? Running counter to much of today’s on-demand culture, yearning melds desire and distance, nostalgia and uncertainty; longing for something, or someone, can sometimes appeal in a way that getting exactly what you want cannot. The resurgence of yearning – especially in the romantic sense – has been one of the biggest entertainment themes of the last couple of years: from The Summer I Turned Pretty and Heated Rivalry to the latest big-screen adaptation of Sense and Sensibility , the allure of unmet desire and slow-burn love has topped hasty happy-ever-afters. TikTok remains awash with recommendations for those who want to #feeltheyearn. Continue reading...

item.title: ‘I was in a darker place than I’d ever been. ECT was my only hope’: how Ted Scheinman finally broke through his depression
item.description: Troubled from the age of three, by 35 the American journalist viewed himself as ‘the lowest piece of dirt on the Earth’ – and neither therapy nor drugs seemed to help. But there was one thing he hadn’t tried … Ted Scheinman can date the origin of his depression with laser accuracy. It was the day he went to the fair, aged three, and returned to his home in upstate New York clutching a Batman toy that he’d won. In the bathroom, he swooped his new doll over the sink. Scheinman had a vivid imagination; in a few years, he would want to become a playwright. To add sound effects and drama, he turned on the tap. There was a whoosh – and the unthinkable happened. Water landed on Batman’s pristine boot in a darkening, enlarging spot that for young Scheinman triggered several rapid thoughts, the last of them being: “I am going to die.” Now 41, Scheinman, a senior editor at Smithsonian magazine , has written a memoir of his “life as a depressive”. item.description: Is it ever OK to leave your family – including small children – to live in the wilderness or walk around the world? The latest season of Alone – the US TV competition in which cocky survivalists are dropped into a remote, inhospitable wilderness only to be rapidly humbled by squirrels and their own colons – has just ended. I love Alone. The landscapes are spectacular and their implacable hostility to humans obscurely cheering; plus, I get real atavistic satisfaction from watching my favourite contestants make shelters or manage to trap rabbits (grim, but at least every scrap of every creature is usually used – someone even ate a hare’s partially digested stomach contents once). I’m also gripped by what it says about being a man. item.title: The efficiency trap: why optimising everything can backfire, badly
item.description: From roundabouts to the stock market, relentless streamlining could be making the world more dangerous We have all been there: packed shoulder to shoulder on the train while the person beside us coughs and sneezes. A protective flu jab offers some reassurance, but so does the thought that there will be a hospital bed for you, should you need it. Yet, in England, about 95% of adult hospital beds were occupied at the height of flu season last year. If hospitals were hotels, that level of occupancy would be good business, and we would commend them for their efficiency. But do we really want a hospital to have so few beds in reserve that it’s just one bad flu week away from having to treat patients in corridors? Continue reading...

I love the idea of kids buying a book, going on holiday and seeing that I’ve signed it. Sometimes I write ‘surprise!’” It’s a wonder that she hasn’t got sore hands. Pichon is one of the UK’s foremost children’s authors, and this is a big year for her. item.title: There is no ‘magic pill’ to fix young women’s anxiety. I should know – I once took propranolol myself | Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett
item.description: Prescriptions for these beta blockers are soaring among England’s teenage girls. But they deserve more than this sticking-plaster approach The first time I had a panic attack, I genuinely thought I was dying. Unless you have experienced one, it is hard to understand just how physical the symptoms can be – the pounding heart, the shortness of breath, the dizziness, the chest pain, the nausea. When they became frequent, I would often have to go to bed to sleep them off, my body utterly spent from the strain of sheer, corporeal terror. A panic attack is not a physical state that I would wish on anyone. It is pure fight or flight. Like many others, I was prescribed a drug called propranolol to help with my anxiety symptoms. Propranolol is a beta blocker used in cardiac patients to lower the heart rate, but it is increasingly prescribed to those with anxiety disorders because it has some calming effects, and can soothe symptoms such as sweating and shaking. That sultry Mumbai evening, Andrew Flintoff sprinted across the outfield twirling his shirt round his head as England won by five runs – a sight that so annoyed captain Sourav Ganguly that he would take his revenge on the Lord’s balcony later that summer. I wrote my report for a local tabloid, the Afternoon Despatch & Courier, with trepidation and an overwhelming sense of impostor syndrome. It’s dawn and we’re chugging through the snaking Preak Piphot River towards the starting point of a 9-mile (15km) overnight trek into the country’s sacred, spirit-filled Cardamom mountain range. The region, a six-hour bus ride west of the capital Phnom Penh, recently made global news for being home to a raft of new species of fauna and a sanctuary for rare and endangered wildlife . item.description: With the global tide turning against him, the US president’s lame duck status could still aggravate old tensions and spark new explosions It was a victory for the world, too. People in the many countries that suffered pain, loss and cruel indignities at the hands of Donald Trump over the past two chaotic, fearful years celebrated a moment of glorious, shared redemption. The monster, like others of his kind, still lurks in his gilded White House lair; far-right authoritarianism still casts a dark shadow over many nations. item.title: Amy Winehouse inspired me to quit a soul-crushing job
item.description: I was driving to work feeling miserable when Rehab came on – and I realised there’s more to life than a steady wage in a job you despise At 6am on a bleak October morning in 2006, I was driving down the North Circular in London to a job I hated. I usually kept the radio low, a background murmur to keep me focused on the road. But that morning I turned up the volume allowing the buoyant bassline from Amy Winehouse’s Rehab to reverberate through my Ford Ka. As Amy’s rich voice conveyed the depths of her despair, I stared blearily at the empty road ahead and wondered how I’d taken such a wrong turn. It was a disorienting time for me. Two years out of uni, I’d accepted a job in the back end of London’s Docklands area, in a freezing cold, windowless office, staring at four giant screens to check whether any of the world’s stock exchanges had technical faults. Yeoh, who is 64, has played grandes dames, action heroes and a low-income Chinese-American battling the tax authorities in an infinite multiverse, but Blade Runner was different. The sci-fi series, a follow-up of sorts to Ridley Scott’s 1982 movie classic and its 2017 sequel , features both humans and replicants, their bioengineered antagonists, and Yeoh was adamant: “I don’t want to be human.” After working on ideas of what a synthetic human might look like, the result is Olwen, a terrifying individual with “a very cold, steely look in her eyes. item.title: Albania’s restored stone houses throw open the doors to visitors
item.description: A project to convert the country’s traditional kulla houses into guesthouses offers a true flavour of ancient hospitality in a part of the country almost untouched by tourism Sunlight pours through a tiny stone window, causing the wooden floorboards to creak as they warm up. The sound of sheep’s bells filters in from a passing flock. The scent of baking bread mingles with smoke from the previous evening’s fire. I wake up feeling I’ve been transported back to another time – but in reality I’m in modern-day Albania. I’m staying in a kulla , one of the traditional stone tower houses that are found throughout northern Albania, Montenegro and North Macedonia. They once protected families during times of conflict and sheltered weary travellers on trade routes, before mostly falling into disrepair in the 20th century. Here is an actor not only at the top of her game, but quite frankly at the top of anybody’s. Her Apple TV show Platonic all but depends on her combination of emotional nuance and flawless slapstick to exist, and earlier this year she won a Golden Globe (and was nominated for an Oscar) for her wired, frayed lead performance in If I Had Legs I’d Kick You. In other words, Byrne should be able to make anything she wants. So it’s bizarre that, of all things, she has chosen this. The Good Daughter is a paperback thriller show. item.description: Teenage ultras are increasingly causing disorder and communities fear it will not be long before it becomes something more dangerous It is five past three on Saturday afternoon and the teenage ultras of Hednesford Town are running late. They have arrived in Chester for their team’s National League North fixture and have hailed taxis, determined to make their presence felt at the ground. item.title: Jackson Boxer’s vegetarian recipe for roast beetroot with pickled raisins and blue cheese
item.description: Surprise yourself with the flavours in this roast beetroot spiked with pickled raisins and salty blue cheese It’s not uncommon for people to form negative relationships with certain vegetables as a consequence of only ever having had them boiled to disintegration, a blunt approach that’s unlikely to bring out the best in any of us. Beetroot, especially, are vastly improved by being roasted instead, because that way they cook gently in their own juices. Not only does this much improve their texture, but it concentrates their innate, earthy richness, rather than leaching out of them. Beetroot’s high level of natural sweetness makes it a perfect foil for sharp dressings and even sharper cheeses. Jackson Boxer is chef/owner of Brunswick House , Vesper and Dove , all in London, and culinary director of Cowley Manor near Cheltenham and the Henrietta in London Continue reading...

But if a trip to the spa seems like too much effort or money, then good news! An alternative could be waiting for you right behind your bathroom door: hot baths. This was true in two senses. Figuratively, because he had been set up by a friend, and quite literally – since his back was gushing blood, as he saw reflected in the pub toilet mirror. It was 2010 and hours earlier, he had been at a street festival in south London. Life was looking up: he had just achieved good exam grades (14 GCSEs) and things were going well with his girlfriend. item.title: ‘I’m never going to be bloody Robert De Niro!’: Rob Brydon, the most chipper man on TV

That’s who I am.” It’s an unnecessary clarification – at 61, he’s been nice on TV, as himself and in character, for most of our adult lives. We’re here to talk about his new six-parter, Bill’s Included, but his character in it, the eponymous Bill, is such a distillation of pure Rob Brydon that it’s (accidentally, he says) a celebration of his entire career. As the show opens, Bill has just been left by his wife, who’s run off with the gardener. At no point does he ever fire the guy – “I like him!” – but otherwise, his life is completely upended. item.title: ‘I went into a deep, deep hole’: Wynonna Judd on overcoming family tragedy and putting a lifetime of love and pain into her new album

Which is a good thing, as the Nashville star has been off the radar for a decade. On the occasions her name has made the news, it’s more often been linked to family tragedy than music. “I’m in a good place,” says the woman Rolling Stone described as “the greatest female country singer since Patsy Cline”. “My life has been chaotic. When the clock strikes midnight, the lavish 4K Switch 2 remake of beloved N64 classic The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time will be released, and I have joined a lengthy queue of about 500 fans desperate to snag early copies. There are similar events taking place across the world, from Melbourne to Mexico City; at key locations, Nintendo has senior executives waiting at the tills. I was lucky enough to come from a home full of books and when we joined my father out at sea for extended periods of time, my mother carried plenty of books for me to read. I remember sitting by the porthole in our cabin, looking out at the sea on a sunny day, the ship moving calmly through the waters. item.title: Songs from the Firefront by Tim Winton review – climate urgency verges on panic, with moments of wonder too
item.description: The masterful Australian writer has become a kind of prophet – and his dramatic and moving new essay collection challenges us not to look away Tim Winton has been working his themes for almost 50 years in a palimpsest of 32 books: family, manhood, land and ocean; what it is to be human and Australian; intimate pleasures and anxieties that feed his fiction. The distinctive quality of his new collection of memoir and essays, Songs from the Firefront, is urgency verging on panic. He’s an elder in his 60s, with limited time to get his messages across before we all go up in flames. Living on the western edge of Australia, Winton has been an eloquent climate-change activist for decades . He has fought, with tenuous success, to protect Ningaloo Reef. He entrances us with Scheherazade stories that blend crystalline nature writing and terrifying facts. The loss has accelerated now, he says, and the danger is immediate. item.title: My childhood was one of survival and resilience. How can I model a joyful life for my kids? | Leading questions
item.description: Start with the feeling, not the activities, writes advice columnist Eleanor Gordon-Smith . Making more room for enjoyment is also making more room for your actual self Read more Leading questions I’m a child of first-generation immigrants and have always carried a story of survival and resilience. My parents were part of a “lost generation” who sacrificed a lot to put us all through university . There was a very defined path for success, some of which I followed and some not. I married outside of race; I made work choices for financial stability . I don’t know how to enjoy things that other people seem to. Hobbies, travelling, home renovations … I look at those like “what is the point?” I want to say it’s because my upbringing was not full of leisure activities; my parents only allowed us to focus on academic topics. Now that I’m a mother though, I wonder how I can role model some of this “living well for its own sake” for my children. It’s hard to find simple joys actually joyful. Gro

item.title: Cristiano Ronaldo merely the latest example of a great player who couldn’t let go | Jonathan Wilson
item.description: There is no doubt his international career was an incredible one, but it would have been greater still if he had not lingered on the stage so long Nothing, perhaps, is quite so difficult for an elite sportsperson as timing their exit. It’s not easy for any person in any job to weigh the hope of having more to give with the desire not to linger beyond their usefulness, but it’s perhaps particularly hard for top athletes because unrealistic self-confidence is so essential to their success. It takes an almost unhealthy level of self-belief for anybody to make the sacrifices to get to the top, to dedicate themselves to such a precarious vocation, to overcome all the setbacks and injuries and failures. How can someone – whose whole life has been spent assuring themselves there are no odds they cannot overcome – accept that is it, that the time has come to say goodbye? item.title: 400,000-year-old teeth reveal a stunning twist in human evolution
item.description: A groundbreaking discovery is rewriting the story of human evolution, revealing that an ancient human species once thought to be an evolutionary dead end may have left genetic traces in people alive today. That genetic connection may have eventually reached modern populations in the Philippines, Papua New Guinea, and other parts of Southeast Asia.

Sign up here Earlier this year, I was stuck in hospital for several days, fuzzy on pain medication and bored out of my mind, with nothing but a Steam Deck for company. In the middle of one of those long nights, unable to sleep, I played a game called Titanium Court . It’s a strange creation that looks like it was made for the ZX Spectrum and reads like a postmodern Shakespeare adaptation – a compelling mix of strategy game and match-3 where you rearrange battlefields by matching tiles, before sending tiny lo-fi fairy armies to their deaths. Rather than evolving for a specific advantage, this unusual arrangement may simply be a legacy of evolution building new brain circuits on an ancient foundation.

item.title: NASA is racing against time to save the Hubble Space Telescope
item.description: NASA is exploring a daring plan to save the legendary Hubble Space Telescope from its eventual fiery plunge into Earth's atmosphere. After more than 35 years of groundbreaking discoveries, Hubble is slowly losing altitude, and without intervention, it could fall back to Earth as early as 2033 or 2034. To keep the iconic observatory operating, NASA is asking private space companies to propose innovative ways to boost Hubble into a higher orbit, upgrade its capabilities, or safely dispose of it when its mission finally ends.

item.title: SLAC scientists find conclusive proof of a mysterious third type of magnetism
item.description: For nearly 90 years, scientists believed magnetism fell into just two categories, but researchers have now confirmed a remarkable third type called altermagnetism. Using specialized X-rays, they uncovered a unique magnetic signature that proves these materials behave differently from conventional magnets. Altermagnets combine stability with the ability to efficiently carry information, potentially overcoming major limitations in today's electronics. The discovery could lead to faster computers, more efficient data centers, and breakthroughs in quantum technology.

item.title: Kids who eat more ultra-processed foods show a troubling brain response
item.description: A new study suggests that ultra-processed foods may influence children's developing brains in ways that encourage weight gain. Researchers from USC studied 46 children ages 7 to 10 and found that those who ate more ultra-processed foods showed stronger activity in the brain's reward system when viewing tempting foods like cookies and French fries. These heightened brain responses were linked to greater increases in body fat and body mass index (BMI) one year later, suggesting that the brain's sensitivity to food cues may help explain why ultra-processed diets are associated with obesity.

item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03593-z Enjoy the month’s best science images. Plus, an outbreak of anthrax in African hippos and the places where biodiversity drops after humans leave.

item.title: Clearing the way for a transformative stem-cell treatment for Parkinson’s disease
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03167-z Most Parkinson’s therapies aim to reduce the motor-control symptoms that the disease triggers. But stem-cell transplants in the brain could alter the disease at a more fundamental level.

item.title: Progress accelerates in Parkinson’s treatments
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03165-1 Researchers are reporting encouraging results for a disease that affects millions of people worldwide.

item.title: Ecosystems depend on people: don’t abandon them
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03544-8 It might seem counterproductive to put more people in nature, but sometimes human activity nurtures biodiversity.

item.title: See a tardigrade shed its skin — October’s best science images
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03563-5 The month’s sharpest science shots, selected by Nature’s photo team.

item.title: Fruit, flies and getting frisky: how food odours trigger sexual arousal
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03271-0 Males of a Drosophila species that thrives on a particular fruit need the smell of food to begin courtship. This environmental cue acts on defined mating circuits in the brain.

item.title: Six highlights from Parkinson’s disease research
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03172-2 Targeting a new network, addressing gait issues and other advances from recent studies.

item.title: Cutting-edge technique uncovers how the spine’s shock absorbers bear load
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03264-z An exciting imaging approach reveals how discs of soft tissue in the spine respond to compressive force at the micrometre and nanometre scales.

item.title: Epileptic seizures nearly vanish after people receive experimental gene therapy in their brains
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03566-2 A clinical trial in three people tested a combination of gene-laden viruses and a drug.

item.title: A death sentence for ‘sloppy’ cancers
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03269-8 The process of making protein from RNA can go awry in cancer cells. This malfunction might be harnessed to create an effective gene-therapy tool that targets tumours.

item.title: Faint exoplanets detected using computational approach to remove glare from stars
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03295-6 An image-processing framework for detecting exoplanets directly has been developed. The technique overcomes the telescope-stability barrier that has limited previous methods, reveals fainter exoplanets than other approaches can detect and could make imaging exo-Earths easier for future observatories.

item.title: People’s social networks can be unintentionally reshaped during randomized interventions
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03267-w A re-examination of a randomized controlled trial for a health-advice intervention reveals ripple effects and altered relationships in communities in rural Honduras.

item.title: Fine-tuning brain stimulation to fight Parkinson’s disease
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03168-y Neuroscientists are developing a new type of brain implant that will decode every movement and symptom of people with this neurodegenerative condition, seeking better ways to ease symptoms.

item.title: Mysterious anthrax outbreak kills hippos in Africa — raising concerns for human spread
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03580-4 The latest cases, in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, come as the country grapples with ongoing Ebola and cholera outbreaks.

item.title: When humans disappear, biodiversity takes a surprising turn
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03505-1 For decades, conservation has worried about the risks of too many people. In some places, depopulation is the real threat.

item.title: Could chemicals contribute to Parkinson’s?
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03170-4 Researchers and advocates point to pollutants as a trigger for the neurodegenerative condition.

item.title: Replacing the neurons that Parkinson’s destroys
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03166-0 After decades of work, researchers have begun trialling transplants of dopamine neurons into people with the neurodegenerative disease — with early signs of success.

item.title: Why are we conscious? Nature investigates the theories
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03413-4 Scientists have yet to reveal how the human brain produces the subjective experience we perceive as consciousness, but research has pushed the field in exciting directions.

item.title: Infrared image detectors grown directly on read-out chips
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03420-5 A film of lead sulfide — an infrared-sensitive semiconductor — has been grown directly on a circuit that can read out the material’s electrical signal through an approach called monolithic in situ integration. This brings material growth and electronic integration together into a single step. The resulting image sensor shows high sensitivity for infrared wavelengths.

item.title: A two-dimensional reticular triaxial molecularly woven fabric
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11218-8 A two-dimensional reticular triaxial woven network material is constructed by incorporating C3-symmetric macrocycles into a triangular weave pattern, enabling an extra topological dimension to be used for the construction of functional materials.

item.title: Accelerating commercialization and deployment of indoor photovoltaics
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11133-y Recent progress in photovoltaics has been investigated to translate state-of-the-art cells in the laboratory into deployable products suited to real indoor conditions, focusing on wide-bandgap absorbers, reduced non-radiative voltage losses and reshaping module design.

item.title: In vivo CAR-T double knockout screen maps synergistic antitumour gene pairs
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10956-z Using high-throughput in vivo CAR-T double knockout screening, synergistic gene combinations to improve CAR-T cell therapy are revealed.

item.title: Observation of prethermal dynamical phase transitions and resonant melting
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11225-9 A programmable neutral-atom quantum simulator is used to explore quench dynamics in spin models with up to 180 qubits, revealing prethermal dynamical phase transitions and resonant melting.

item.title: Ecological and social cues orchestrate concerted courtship in Drosophila
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11209-9 In Drosophila erecta, food odours initiate male sexual arousal, which is subsequently reinforced by the visual motion of other courting flies, creating a multisensory mechanism that synchronizes courtship in groups when conditions are favourable for reproduction.

item.title: An AI-native experimental laboratory for autonomous biomolecular operations
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11228-6 AutoDNA is an artificial intelligence (AI)-native autonomous biomolecular engineering laboratory targeting multi-objective experiments across diverse instruments, realizing the co-evolution of AI and the automation system within an end-to-end multi-user framework.

item.title: Multimodal X-ray imaging reveals hierarchical fibre mechanics
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11148-5 The X-ray visualization platform TomoSAXS, demonstrated here on intervertebral spinal discs, can visualize nanoscale to macroscale mechanics in intact biological organs and fibrous materials.

item.title: Towards observing interstitial hydrogen in solution in metal lattices
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11238-4 Using deuterium as a proxy for hydrogen, atom probe tomography provides experimental evidence for interstitial hydrogen in solid solution across different FCC phases, consistent with theoretical predictions of hydrogen affinity, revealing hydrogen partitioning in structural alloys.

item.title: Decoding the regulatory programs governing glioblastoma plasticity
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11177-0 Multi-omic analyses of cells from patients with glioblastoma (GB) provide insight into the role of non-genetic cellular plasticity in disease progression, showing that state stability in GB cells is controlled by a network of interacting activators and repressors.

item.title: Comprehensive mapping of essential-gene interactions in M. tuberculosis
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11212-0 A high-throughput CRISPR-interference platform allows the mapping of interactions between essential genes in Mycobacterium tuberculosis, revealing many previously unknown genetic interactions and providing insight into gene function and drug–target relationships that could enable the development of new therapies for tuberculosis.

item.title: Conjugation-regulated self-assembled molecules for tandem solar cells
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11226-8 Rationally engineered molecular spatial conjugation is used for the formation of highly ordered, conformal self-assembled molecules, enabling the fabrication of high-performance perovskite/silicon tandem solar cells.

item.title: Hard X-ray attosecond metrology
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11245-5 Metrology techniques are developed to characterize and control attosecond hard X-ray pulses, directly measuring a 170-attosecond duration and enabling ultrafast studies of electronic dynamics in quantum systems.

item.title: Cancer-selective gene circuits via intrinsic ribosomal frameshifting
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11200-4 Codon-pair-dependent ribosomal frameshifting is a feature of translational dysregulation in cancer cells.

item.title: Tracing the spread of Celtic languages using ancient genomics
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11198-9 Genome-wide data from 4,587 ancient individuals are analysed, focusing on Bronze and Iron Age Europe, to test the extent to which alternative archaeological and linguistic models for the origin and spread of Celtic fit reconstructed demographic histories.

item.title: Venousization enables angiogenesis in the absence of VEGFR signalling
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11224-w Longitudinal tracking of endothelial cells shows they can adapt to loss of VEGFR2 and form new functional vessels, challenging conventional views of the essential role of VEGF receptors in angiogenesis and providing insight into resistance to anti-VEGF therapies.

item.title: The neural basis of flavour–nutrient learning
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11229-5 A dopamine pathway to the basolateral amygdala is necessary for associating nutrients with flavours.

item.title: Nectin-4 mediates rubella virus entry in airway and placental cells
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11248-2 Nectin-4 is identified as a pivotal host entry receptor for respiratory transmission and early placental infection of rubella virus.

item.title: Aggression experience and observation drive shared behavioural and neural changes
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11217-9 Aggression experience and observation recruit a brain-wide network of excitatory, inhibitory and valence signals, and changes to this activation pattern predict a shared adaptive behaviour-control policy in a new aggression context.

item.title: Transcriptomic convergence and the female protective effect in autism
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11236-6 Gene network analysis shows how mutations in diverse genes associated with autism spectrum disorder can converge to exert shared effects, with X-linked transcription factor ZFX emerging as a key protective factor in the female brain.

item.title: The deep Earth origin of the Great Unconformity
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11156-5 Continental-scale uplift and subsidence associated with long-wavelength dynamic topography due to mantle convection drove the formation and preservation of the Great Unconformity.

item.title: Twist-angle-dependent quantum phase diagrams in moiré bilayer MoTe<sub>2</sub>
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11274-0 Twist-angle-dependent studies of moiré bilayer MoTe2 reveal a transition from fractional topological states to correlated insulators and superconductivity, linking topology, symmetry breaking and magnetism in moiré quantum materials.

item.title: An open structure-guided RNA foundation model for generalizable prediction
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11210-2 structRFM, a structure-guided RNA foundation model pre-trained on 21 million sequence–structure pairs, learns multimodal representations that improve secondary and tertiary structure prediction, functional inference and zero-shot generalization across diverse RNA families.

item.title: Synergy in viral–bacterial co-infection expedites algal bloom demise
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11243-7 Viral–bacterial synergy accelerates algal bloom collapse by enhancing virus-induced mortality, driven by Alteromonas chemoattraction and co-infection, revealing a previously unrecognized mortality agent that influences oceanic carbon cycling .

item.title: A conserved flowering-time module underlies double-season cropping
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11187-y The genomic footprints of 80 years of modern breeding in China are traced using representative cultivars, demonstrating how precision genome editing can be used to reconstruct adaptive modules for climate-resilient crop design.

item.title: Microbiome-wide PheWAS links gut microbial SNVs to health and exposures
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11220-0 Gut microbial single-nucleotide variants across 10,781 individuals reveal 940 associations that link strain-level genetic variation to 69 host traits, with structural analyses pinpointing host phenotype-associated variants, providing a base pair-resolution resource for mechanistic hypothesis generation.

item.title: A spatiotemporal cancer cell trajectory underlies glioblastoma heterogeneity
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11234-8 A deep single-cell and spatial multi-omic atlas of human glioblastoma is generated, pairing transcriptomic, epigenomic and genomic profiling, and tracing glioblastoma tumour heterogeneity to a stereotyped and spatially patterned trajectory of cancer cells.

item.title: The brain’s hidden fear mechanism may explain anxiety and PTSD
item.description: A surprising new discovery suggests that fear may cause the brain to blur the line between danger and safety rather than distinguish them more clearly. By observing brain activity in mice using augmented reality, scientists found that memories of threatening and harmless environments began to overlap, potentially allowing faster responses to danger. This "better safe than sorry" survival mechanism could help explain why people with anxiety or PTSD sometimes experience intense fear in completely safe situations.

item.title: A 50-year-old mystery of vanishing frogs reveals a hidden killer
item.description: A nearly 50-year-old mystery involving disappearing frogs in Brazil may finally be solved, with scientists uncovering evidence that a deadly fungus swept through the region and devastated vulnerable species. Remarkably, many frog populations have since rebounded, suggesting they developed greater tolerance to the disease that once threatened their survival.

Now he’s done a knee slide too, and in the perfect place: back where it all began and where it can all begin again. When Kylian Mbappé scored the first in the clásico on Sunday night, Real Madrid’s manager hardly moved, sitting in the shadow of the bench – but when the striker got the second to win it with time running out, that was different. Mourinho leapt into the light, throwing himself to the grass, the knees of a 63-year-old’s trousers muddy as a schoolboy’s, stuck his tongue out and pumped his fists. He does so love it when a plan comes together. To the right of him, the bench was emptying, subs joining the players in sprinting towards the south-west corner. item.description: Swindon manager has a history of viral outbursts but fans want a united club and manager they can support In Ian Holloway’s often madcap managerial orbit, this was simply the latest in a steady succession of eccentric outbursts. Eyes bulging as he spoke, he boomed the letter “D” and promptly stabbed himself in the chest with an imaginary dagger. Next came the letter “M” alongside a blow from another invisible knife. Finally, a “W” followed by a jab to the heart. “Dead. Man. Walking,” he declared, pausing for effect between words and briefly falling into an Oscar-worthy zombie stupor. “That’s how it feels.” To an offbeat press conference genre containing seagulls following trawlers and self-proclaimed special ones, it was a crazy new entry worthy of its subsequent viral nature. item.title: Transfer window verdict: how every Premier League club fared
item.description: The British transfer record was equalled and one club signed no fewer than 18 players in another hectic summer Bringing in Christos Tzolis, Bruno Guimarães and Ezri Konsa was a strong start to the window but could Arsenal’s failure to sign a marquee attacker cost them in the long run? They began targeting Morgan Rogers before pivoting to Vinícius Júnior when the England forward went to Chelsea, only to end up disappointed when Vinícius signed a new deal with Real Madrid. Julián Alvarez made clear he had no intention of joining from Atlético Madrid in the final days of the window and Arsenal kept their powder dry despite sanctioning the exits of Gabriel Jesus to Barcelona and Ethan Nwaneri to Borussia Dortmund. Should Gabriel Martinelli complete his move to Al-Hilal as expected in the coming days – the Saudi Pro League window remains open – a few injuries could leave Arteta short. item.title: Ousmane Dembélé quietly becomes the main man after long journey to the top
item.description: The Frenchman, who has been named the best male footballer in the world by the Guardian, has benefitted from PSG’s focus on the team rather than individuals What makes a good player great, and a great player the best? This question has been occupying me since 2014, when the Guardian first asked me to contribute to its inaugural Next Generation feature . My job was to look for a France-based talent born in 1997 who could go on to have a stellar career. After a great deal of research, I narrowed it down from my shortlist of five by asking questions not about the players’ football ability, but about other attributes: resilience, adaptability, decision-making, creativity, work ethic, response to feedback and willingness to learn. Qualities we cannot see, and are harder to measure. Continue reading...

item.title: Aitana Bonmatí makes Guardian top 100 history with third title in a row
item.description: The margin may have got smaller but the brilliant Spanish midfielder makes it a hat-trick of No 1 finishes They say the best things come in threes, and Aitana Bonmatí has written herself into the Guardian’s top 100 history as the first player to finish at the top of the tree for a third consecutive year. Last year the majestic midfielder emulated her Barcelona and Spain teammate Alexia Putellas by winning for a second year running , but the 27-year-old has now gone one better, establishing herself once again at the top of the women’s game.
